name: Miskies AI
tagline: Consumer AI app that turns uploaded photos into stylized characters and cute renders through a one-tap flow.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Consumer AI image apps in this shape are almost always a hosted image model plus a good prompt, a clean upload screen, and a paywall. None of those three things are hard for an agent to reproduce, and the model doing the actual work is rented by both you and them. Where the product wins is taste: the exact prompt and style presets that make output look consistently cute rather than uncanny, which you will spend a few iterations rediscovering. If the app turns out to be doing something heavier, like fulfilling physical products or running its own fine-tuned model, downgrade this to kinda and pay attention to the fulfillment side rather than the software.
coreLoopDIY: Upload a photo, pick a style preset, hit a hosted image model with a tuned prompt, and get a downloadable render back plus a local gallery of past results.
requirements: An API key for a hosted image model that supports image input (Gemini image, OpenAI images, or Replicate)
Willingness to pay per generation instead of per month
whatYouLose: Style presets that someone already tuned across thousands of real user photos, so your first outputs will look worse
A polished mobile experience: camera capture, share sheet, no cold-start friction
Any hosted history, cross-device sync, or a link you can send to a friend
Whatever guardrails and face-handling they added after users broke things
If they ship physical merch from the renders, the entire fulfillment chain
moatNotes: The defensible part is prompt taste and the app store distribution, not the pixels. Both are copyable, one is just tedious.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a subscription is cheaper than the twenty minutes and three API keys it takes to discover that your own prompt makes everyone look slightly melted. Novelty image apps are impulse purchases: the value is having a fun result in ten seconds on a phone, not owning the pipeline. A self-hosted version is strictly better if you generate a lot and worse in every way if you generate twice and forget about it.
notes: Thin wrappers around rented image models are the easiest category on this site to replace, and the hardest to replace well on the first try.
prompt:
Build a local web app called "plushbench" that turns an uploaded photo into a stylized character render.

Stack, no substitutions: Vite + React + TypeScript on the front end, a small Express server in the same repo for the model calls, plain CSS, no UI framework, no database.

Server:
- POST /api/generate accepts a multipart image plus a style id.
- It calls a hosted image model that accepts an input image (use the Google Gemini image generation API; read GEMINI_API_KEY from .env via dotenv).
- Style presets live in one file, styles.ts, as id + label + prompt template. Ship four: crochet plushie, vinyl figure, felt keychain, claymation.
- Write the returned image to ./output/YYYY-MM-DD-HHMMSS-style.png and return the filename as JSON.
- Serve ./output statically so results load in the browser.
- Never store the uploaded original on disk; keep it in memory only.

Front end:
- One page. Drag-and-drop or file picker, a row of style buttons, a Generate button, a big result image with a Download link.
- Below it, a gallery of everything already in ./output, newest first, read from GET /api/history.
- Show a real loading state and show the actual server error text when a call fails. No fake progress bars.

Explicitly out of scope: accounts, auth, payments, telemetry, cloud storage, deployment config, Docker, tests beyond one smoke test that the server boots.

Include a .env.example with GEMINI_API_KEY=, a .gitignore covering .env and output/, and a README with two commands: install and dev. Add one README section called "Tuning" explaining that output quality is almost entirely the prompt templates in styles.ts and that they should be edited by hand after looking at real results.
